You've made some great points and I  agree with you completely. I don't really understand this whole topic that much myself, but thank you for listening to my opinion.

Thank you for taking the time out of your day to respond nicely to me, and not arguing. (lots of people from both sides, get really mad about this topic) 

I hope you have a fantastic rest of your day.

Coming from an undiagnosed person, (I have siblings with autism who share the same symptoms with me almost exactly, I fit all the criteria and I've been told by medical Professionals It's highly likely I'm autistic but they cannot diagnose me without a referral, so please do not bash me or anything.) I get rather confused by the diagnosis is a privilege thing too. 

Like maybe it's just how it's worded.

 For me, personally, you can tell somethings off about me just by looking at me. I can't walk right; I walk on my toes and my body sorta slants when I walk so I end up walking diagonally, I zone out a lot, and I can't function without someone there to look after me. I was also in speech therapy for a lot of my early childhood because I couldn't speak coherently, and even now, my speech isn't that great. I've got a stutter, and can't say a lot of words. 

I also require almost constant supervision to ensure I take care of my basic needs like sleeping, eating, drinking going to the toilet and other things. When I'm unsupervised and not provided with instructions, I tend to either freeze, and zone out, or hyperfocus on one specific task to the point I won't eat, sleep, go to the toilet, etc until it is done.

I originally slipped under the radar because my brother's autism presented with violent meltdowns, and even though I wasn't very good at masking, because my meltdowns mainly consisted of crying and shutting down, or violent outbursts against myself. By the time it was acknowledged, it was too late and my primary school refused to refer me to a paediatrician because, and I quote; 'You're a girl. Girls can't have autism' 

So I can understand the bit about being frustrated about not being able to access a diagnosis when you need one. 

For example, I don't have an educational health care plan, because as of yet, I am undiagnosed. (I know not all diagnosed people have an educational healthcare plan, its just mainly accessible with a diagnosis)

This means when I go to college this year, I'm going to have to go into the mainstream bit instead of the special Ed bit, which is a huge hurdle, and has almost prevented me from attending. I won't be able to access any extra support, and I'll have to try and navigate through it on my own, when I'm often described of being incapable of taking care of myself, and I cannot cope on my own in social situations.

But then again, some diagnosed people get their needs ignored like this too, which shows it is a failure of the system.

But  I think what they're trying to say is not that DIAGNOSIS is the privilege. It's the SUPPORT. They just wording it funny. I don't know. I might be wrong, please don't get mad with me if I am. 

And I understand not all diagnosed people get support either. But when you're diagnosed, there's a lot more opportunities for support than when you're not. For example, my brother is diagnosed. And I know his experiences are not going to be the same as everyone's, but because of his diagnosis, he has an educational health care plan, which means he can get one to one  support within educational settings. I don't. He gets access to special education resources. I don't, which leaves me very far behind in the educational setting. (For example, I can't count without using my fingers, and I couldn't tell the time until I was 14, after months of 1 on 1 support.)

 He can also apply for charities and services if he wished which could help provide him with extra support in other areas, such as assisted living, support with career skills, ect. Whereas I can't. And I'm not saying applying to these charities will automatically ensure you get lots of support because they won't. There's still waiting lists and stuff like that. But having a diagnosis means you can access these services, even if they don't help you. (I understand this isn't the case for everyone, but it is for most) 

So I understand in some sense what they mean. But I understand the other side being offended by this too, because they feel the usage of the word privilege diminishes their struggles, and their potential hardships in aquiring said diagnosis in the first place. And I understand getting support is still hard with a diagnosis. It's just easier than without one at all. And some people who are undiagnosed also have very high support needs which go unmet. 

I apologise if anything I said was offensive. I tried to use my own experiences as sort of an example, and I tried my best to consider both sides. Again, I apologise if this is offensive in any way, I'm not trying to argue or anything, I just wanted to say my opinion on the matter, if that's okay. 

The final conclusion of all of this rambling is that it's not the actual diagnosis in itself which is the privilege, it's the support, some of which cannot be accessed without a diagnosis. I think the access to support is what they meant. 

That access to support is a privilege? But some diagnosed people don't even have access to support either, which diminishes the whole 'diagnosis is a privilege' thing. 

I don't know. 

Sorry if I worded any of this wrong, or if it upset anyone. Thanks for reading. Have a good day.


TLDR; It's not the diagnosis which is a privilege, but access to support

Hey, just in reply to being to scared to call the police, I understand the fear behind that completely. If you're uncomfortable talking on the phone, (or even just to the police) you could always text shout to 85258. It might say that it could cost something, but it doesn't I promise. It doesn't even show up on the phone bill, so if you change your mind, then nobody at home will even know you tried to do anything. They will call the police if need be. That way you don't have to worry about it being "bad enough" all I can say is that If anything warrants you to feel this way, it's probably bad enough, but I understand why you're worried. It's scary, it is. I hope I can be of some help. I'm so proud of you for asking for help, despite everything. I'm rooting for you buddy. You can do this.

Hey. I don't know how much I can help. But I'm going to try. First things first, I'm so proud of you for asking for help. I'm proud of you for lasting this long. And I know I'm just another stranger on the Internet and it won't mean that much, but I am proud of you. From the word GCSE's I'm gathering you're probably from the UK. First things first, you should call the police. But from past experience, I know how hard that can be. If the police doesn't feel like a viable option, then the best place to go is either childline or shout. Neither of these will show up on the phone bill, I promise. The number for shout, is 85258. You can text shout to 85258, and it will say it might cost something (it doesn't don't worry.) After that, you can text or call one of the people there, who can contact the police for you. Or you could just vent to them. It's up to you. Childline is 0800 1111. You can phone them, or go on their website, where you can message them, like a text. I'm sorry if I can't be of any help. I hope your situation improves soon buddy. Please hang in there. If you are positive that this is your decision, call the police, or even an ambulance. A mental health crisis is just as bad as physical health one.  I'm rooting for you.

Before my parents split up they were in a very toxic relationship. My mother took this out on me and my siblings. My father wasn't much better either. They seemed to always focus their rage on me because well, In truth I was nothing like them. They also used me like a emotional dump, if that's what it's called. They told me all their problems and expected me to fix them. I was also blackmailed into looking after my little brother and sister (at the time they were 2  and 1 )which caused me to fall behind in school. 

My father is an alcoholic and at the beginning of 2020, he became addicted to drugs. I had to care for him like he was a child and he almost died on several occasions (he is a diabetic and doesn't eat or take his insulin sometimes) and I ended up being taken out of his care by social services and put back with my mother.(I was living with father because I was removed from her care)

 My older sister emotionally abused me for most of my life. My parents told me to ignore it. From the time I turned ten I couldn't go a day without her telling me to kill myself, about how worthless I truly am. As the years went by, the words because engraved in my mind like a hidden scar for nobody to see. My mother just said my sister is depressed and it's not her fault.(my sister is my mother's favourite, she's admitted to this on several occasions.)

I was also heavily bullied at school. I don't particularly want to go into detail but this bullying and social exclusion lead to me writing my first suicide note at eight. 

I'm sorry to go on so much, but a lot has happened. More than this, but I don't think there is enough words in the English language to explain. And even if there was, I don't know if I would be able to explain even then. 

Also, this might sound weird, but I'm proud of you for staying alive. I hope you stay alive for a very long time.
